mcqs.question: A senior engineer is confident they know which function is the bottleneck in a slow service, without having profiled it yet this quarter. What should happen next?
options: Trust the assessment — experienced engineers develop reliable intuition for this
Optimize that function first since it's the most likely candidate anyway
Profile the running system before changing anything, treating the guess as unverified
Skip profiling only if the function was the bottleneck in a previous incident
mcqs.explanation: Real profiling sessions repeatedly show the actual hot spot is somewhere the engineer wasn't expecting, because modern systems hide cost behind innocent-looking calls. Confidence, seniority, and past incidents don't change that — the guess has to be tested against a profiler before it's acted on.

mcqs.question: A database batches 100 writes into a single disk flush instead of flushing each write immediately. What does this do to latency and throughput?
options: Both improve, since fewer flushes means less total disk work
Throughput improves, but the first writes in the batch wait longer, worsening their latency
Latency improves for every write, and throughput is unaffected
Neither changes, since the same number of writes eventually reach disk
mcqs.explanation: Batching amortizes the fixed flush cost across many writes, raising throughput — but early writes in the batch now sit waiting for the rest to arrive, so their individual latency rises. This is the canonical latency-vs-throughput trade, not a free win on both axes.

mcqs.question: In a request, 20% of the time is spent in a serial step that cannot be parallelized. According to Amdahl's Law, what is the maximum possible speedup from parallelizing the other 80%, even with unlimited resources?
options: Unlimited — enough parallel resources can drive total time arbitrarily close to zero
5x, since the ceiling is 1 divided by the non-parallelizable fraction
80x, matching the parallelizable percentage
4x, since 80% divided by 20% equals 4
mcqs.explanation: The serial 20% sets a floor: speedup ≤ 1 / (1 − P) = 1 / 0.2 = 5x, no matter how many resources attack the parallel 80%. Throwing infinite cores at the parallel part still leaves the serial part fully intact, capping total speedup at 5x.

mcqs.question: A team shaves 5% off the runtime of ten different functions, none of which is the system's actual bottleneck. What is the likely effect on overall latency?
options: Overall latency drops by roughly 50%, since the improvements compound
Overall latency drops by close to 5%, since averages dominate
Overall latency barely changes, since none of the ten functions dominates the time budget
Overall latency gets worse, since ten simultaneous changes always add risk
mcqs.explanation: Overall speed is set by the dominant contributor to the time budget; improving ten non-bottleneck functions moves the total by close to nothing, while a single 20% win on the actual bottleneck would move the total by roughly 20%. Broad micro-tuning is a common way to burn effort for no visible result.

mcqs.question: What is the actual point of Knuth's "premature optimization is the root of all evil"?
options: Optimization work is generally a waste of engineering time
Code should never be optimized unless a customer files a complaint
Optimizing before measurement identifies the real bottleneck wastes effort and often adds complexity for no benefit
Optimization should be deferred until after the product has shipped
mcqs.explanation: Knuth's full quote explicitly carves out the "critical 3%" as worth optimizing — the warning is against optimizing before you know where that 3% is, which typically adds complexity (caches, hand-inlining) to code that wasn't the bottleneck. It isn't a blanket statement against optimizing at all.

mcqs.question: A team benchmarks a cache-layer optimization using requests that are all cache hits, then ships it. In production, 30% of requests miss the cache. What's the most likely outcome?
options: The optimization performs exactly as the benchmark predicted, since cache logic is deterministic
The optimization's added bookkeeping shows up as pure overhead on the miss path the benchmark never exercised
Cache misses in production will also improve, since the optimization touches shared cache code
The benchmark result is still valid, since cache hit rate doesn't affect optimization outcomes
mcqs.explanation: A benchmark that never exercises the miss path can't tell you how the optimization behaves there — and added bookkeeping that pays off on a hit can be pure overhead on a miss, actively regressing 30% of real traffic. Benchmark traffic has to match production's actual shape to be trustworthy.
